# Mahāsutasomajātaka (Ja 537)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāsutasomajātaka* (Ja 537) is one of the expansive, epic narrative poems of the Pali Jātaka collection, situated in the *Asītinipāta* (eighty-verse nipāta) [Galasek 2016]. According to its traditional frame, the Buddha recounted the tale while residing at Jetavana with reference to the conversion of the bandit Aṅgulimāla, who is identified in the concluding resolution (*samodhāna*) as the former cannibal king Brahmadatta / Kammāsapada (Sanskrit Kalmāṣapāda) [Monius 2001; Galasek 2016]. The central story recounts how this monarch developed an uncontrollable craving for human flesh, was expelled from his realm, and turned to hunting human victims in the forest [DeCaroli 1999; Galasek 2016].

When the cannibal king captures Prince Sutasoma (the Bodhisatta), his former classmate and prince of the Kurus, Sutasoma asks to be temporarily released in order to keep a promise to a brāhmaṇa to whom he had pledged reward for reciting four stanzas preserved from the Buddha Kassapa [Anandajoti 2010; DeCaroli 1999; Galasek 2016]. Sutasoma faithfully returns to face death, an act that traditionally exemplifies the ultimate perfection of truth (*saccapāramī*) [DeCaroli 1999; Gaffney 2003]. Struck by Sutasoma's fearlessness and integrity, the man-eating king grants him boons; Sutasoma utilizes this opportunity to deliver moral instruction on duties, fortune, and mindfulness, successfully persuading the king to renounce cannibalism and orchestrating his peaceful rehabilitation [Anandajoti 2010; DeCaroli 1999].

 DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-corpus reuses, registering substantial internal overlap with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā*, SN 1, and AN 4, as well as alignments with Āryaśūra's Sanskrit and Tibetan *Jātakamālā* [DharmaNexus]. The story is also referenced in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 7.3.10)  and illustrated in traditional temple paintings [IBC 2011].
